An eight-holding mix blending to an 8% yield needs about $1.6 million to pay $11,100 a month without selling shares.

Every holding carries a catch, from volatile payouts at EXG to MPLX's messy K-1 tax form and AT&T's flat dividend.

A 3.5% yield growing 8% a year nearly doubles income by year nine, while a flat 12% yield stalls and loses ground to inflation.

Americans who work with a financial advisor have saved more than twice as much for retirement, on average. Find out what one could change for you: SmartAsset's free quiz matches you with up to three vetted fiduciary advisors in about five minutes. (Sponsor)

You're seeing a paycheck that shows up whether the market rises or falls: $11,100 a month, or $133,200 a year, without ever hitting the sell button.

adamkaz / E+ via Getty Images

Divide the income by the yield to find how much capital the plan requires. Below is an eight-holding blueprint, what each piece does, and the catch that comes with each one.

How Much Money Each Yield Level Demands

At a conservative 3.5% yield from broad dividend growth funds, $133,200 divided by 0.035 equals about $3,806,000. You need the most money, but income usually grows and principal tends to appreciate.

A moderate 6% yield comes from REITs, preferreds, and covered call funds. At a moderate 6% yield, $133,200 divided by 0.06 equals $2,220,000. Dividend growth slows, and some of these strategies cap your upside.

At an aggressive 10% from BDCs and leveraged closed-end funds, $133,200 divided by 0.10 equals $1,332,000. Cuts are more common, and principal can erode.

An 8.3% Blueprint Built on About $1.6 Million

This mix sits between moderate and aggressive. Based on the listed yields, the portfolio blends to 8.31%, so the income target is about $1,603,000. Each 15% slot works out to roughly $241,200, and each 10% slot is about $160,800.

------

Can You Answer These Three Questions?

Americans say they need $1.46 million to retire comfortably. Whether that number fits your life depends on three questions most people never work through:

1. How much can you withdraw each year without running out?

2. When should you claim Social Security?

3. How much will taxes take from your 401(k) or IRA?

A fiduciary advisor can answer all three using your real numbers. SmartAsset's free quiz matches you with up to three who serve your area.

Eaton Vance Tax-Managed Global Diversified Equity Income Fund (NYSE:EXG), 15%. Option income from global stocks, yielding about 9.7%. The catch: the monthly payout has bounced around, from $0.0813 in 2013 to $0.0553 in 2023. Check whether that yield holds up before you count on it.

Global X Super Dividend ETF (NYSEARCA:DIV), 15%. It holds 50 high-dividend-paying U.S. stocks and yields about 6.9%. The catch: monthly payouts were $0.1705 in 2015 and are $0.106 now.

Gaming and Leisure Properties (NASDAQ:GLPI), 15%. A casino landlord yielding about 8.7%, with Q3 AFFO of $1.04 per share covering the $0.82 dividend. The catch: tenants are concentrated, with PENN Entertainment (NASDAQ:PENN) leasing 34 properties.

Capital Southwest (NASDAQ:CSWC), 10%. This BDC lends to small private companies and yields about 9.9% on its regular monthly payout. The catch: non-accruals rose to 1.4%, and every 25-basis-point rate cut trims NII by about $0.06 per share.

MPLX (NYSE:MPLX), 15%. A pipeline partnership yielding about 8.6%. It raised its distribution 13% for the third straight year with 1.3x coverage. One drawback: it sends a K-1 instead of a 1099, which makes filing messier and complicates holding it in an IRA.

AT&T (NYSE:T), 10%. Telecom anchor yielding about 4.8%, supported by free cash flow of $18B+ in 2026. The catch: the dividend stays flat through 2028.

PIMCO Dynamic Income Opportunities Fund (NYSE:PDO), 10%. A leveraged bond fund yielding about 13.5%. The catch: shares fell 8% over the past year. Make sure that yield is real before you lean on it.

iShares 0-3 Month Treasury Bond ETF (NYSEARCA:SGOV), 10%. Your cash cushion, yielding about 3.9%. The catch: payouts follow T-bill rates, and the 13-week bill now yields 4.3%. When the Fed cuts, this check shrinks.

title: Have AT&T's Dividends Been Worth It?
detail:
Have AT&T's Dividends Been Worth It?
Trefis Team
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 6:25 AM EST 3 min read
T
^GSPC
Trade AT&T on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

AT&T sells wireless plans and fiber internet. It pays part of the cash it earns to holders as dividends. Over the past year alone, dividends added about 4.3 percentage points to the stock's return. A percentage point is the plain difference between two returns. The share price, though, has trailed the market. So what did a five-year holder end up with once every dividend is counted?

How Far Has AT&T Stock Trailed The Market?

On price alone, AT&T stock rose 22.8% from November 17, 2021 to November 25, 2026. The S&P 500 rose 53.1% over the same dates. That left AT&T 30.3 percentage points behind. A holder who watched only the price saw the market pull far ahead.

AT&T trailed the market by 30.3 points on its share price alone. If you rely on this one stock to pay your bills, its cash payouts, not its share price, have carried most of your return. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.

How Much Did AT&T's Dividends Add?

With dividends reinvested, AT&T returned 62.5% over the same five years. Reinvested means each payment bought more shares. The dividends added 39.7 percentage points to the price gain. Most of the holder's result came from the dividends, not the share price.

Did The Dividends Close The Gap For AT&T Holders?

The table sets AT&T beside the S&P 500, first on price alone and then with dividends.

The market pays dividends too. With them counted, the S&P 500 returned 63.7%. That leaves AT&T just 1.2 percentage points behind. AT&T's dividends closed almost all of the gap with the market.

What This Means If You Own AT&T For Income

AT&T did pay out more than the market. Over the past year, its dividends added 4.3 points to its return, against 1.2 points for the market's dividends. Over five years, AT&T's larger payments made up for nearly all of the gap its slower share price left.

The cash comes from its phone and internet business, the Communications segment. It brought in 96.2% of revenue in 2025, the year to December 31. In the four quarters to September 30, 2026, AT&T produced $17.8 billion of free cash flow. That is the cash left after running and investing in the business. It paid $7.94 billion in dividends over the same quarters.

The company's October 21 earnings release guides to an annual dividend of $1.11 a share for 2026. A past dividend is a record, not a promise. For an income holder, the test to keep checking is whether AT&T's return with dividends keeps pace with the S&P 500's with dividends.

AT&T Is Up 10% in a Month. Steve Eisman Calls the Big Three Carriers "Uninvestable." Who's Right? ©@9comeback from Getty Images via Canva, @Mohit Khare from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

AT&T stock is up 10% in the past month as the broader market fell and investors moved into cheap, high-yielding stocks.

SpaceX wants to build a fourth US carrier, but the Boost Mobile network it wants to buy runs on AT&T and T-Mobile, which reportedly plan to cut it off.

AT&T's free cash flow covers its dividend more than twice over, and the stock trades at 9.0x forward earnings, right at its 5-year average.

Steve Eisman's "uninvestable" call looks too harsh on AT&T, though AST SpaceMobile's satellite rollout and fourth-quarter churn will show how the SpaceX fight plays out.

AT&T (T:NYSE) stock rose 10% in the month to its Nov. 25 close, while the S&P 500 fell 6% and the Nasdaq 100 fell 10%.

After the close on Oct. 22, Bloomberg reported that SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) was seeking access to at least 80,000 US cell sites to become a fourth carrier, and AT&T and T-Mobile US (TMUS:NASDAQ) each fell about 8% the next day. Since then, both have reportedly pushed back on SpaceX, and AT&T has leaned on its satellite partner, AST SpaceMobile (ASTS:NASDAQ).

Not everyone's buying the rebound. On the Nov. 6 episode of The Real Eisman Playbook, Steve Eisman said of AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile: "I think the big three are just uninvestable."

Income buyers came back

With no big company news, AT&T rode investors' move into steady, high-yielding stocks as tech sold off: Walmart rose 10%, McDonald's 14% and Campbell's more than 15% over the same stretch. Buyers had reason to like AT&T's third quarter. Adjusted EPS rose to $0.65 from $0.54 a year earlier, management raised its 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to about $2.40 from $2.25-$2.35, and it kept its plan for $18 billion-plus of free cash flow. (Management credits most of that raise to halting depreciation on the Mexico unit it's selling.)

Analysts expect normalized EPS to keep rising, from $2.12 in 2025 to $2.93 in 2028:

AT&T (T): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2029 (TIKR)

That's about 11% a year, in line with AT&T's own double-digit guidance.

TIKR tracks 24 analysts on AT&T. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on AT&T, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See AT&T's Analyst Ratings

SpaceX is coming, slowly

The threat is real. Qualcomm's CEO said on its Nov. 4 call that SpaceX chose Qualcomm for a nationwide land-based 5G network starting in 2027, and The Washington Post reported that SpaceX was in talks to buy EchoStar's Boost Mobile. But Boost leases network access from AT&T and T-Mobile, and Semafor reported on Nov. 5 that both would cut Boost off if SpaceX bought it. Even Elon Musk said at the DealBook Summit on Nov. 18: "I don't think this means… AT&T, Verizon, others go out of business or anything."

AT&T (T) has recently been on Zacks.com's list of the most searched stocks. Therefore, you might want to consider some of the key factors that could influence the stock's performance in the near future.

Over the past month, shares of this telecommunications company have returned +9.3%, compared to the Zacks S&P 500 composite's -5% change. During this period, the Zacks Wireless National industry, which AT&T falls in, has lost 6.3%. The key question now is: What could be the stock's future direction?

Although media reports or rumors about a significant change in a company's business prospects usually cause its stock to trend and lead to an immediate price change, there are always certain fundamental factors that ultimately drive the buy-and-hold decision.

Earnings Estimate Revisions

Rather than focusing on anything else, we at Zacks prioritize evaluating the change in a company's earnings projection. This is because we believe the fair value for its stock is determined by the present value of its future stream of earnings.

Our analysis is essentially based on how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to take the latest business trends into account. When earnings estimates for a company go up, the fair value for its stock goes up as well. And when a stock's fair value is higher than its current market price, investors tend to buy the stock, resulting in its price moving upward. Because of this, empirical studies indicate a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and short-term stock price movements.

For the current quarter, AT&T is expected to post earnings of $0.53 per share, indicating a change of +1.9% from the year-ago quarter. The Zacks Consensus Estimate remained unchanged over the last 30 days.

The consensus earnings estimate of $2.4 for the current fiscal year indicates a year-over-year change of +13.2%. This estimate has changed +0.2% over the last 30 days.

For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $2.57 indicates a change of +7.4% from what AT&T is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has remained unchanged.

With an impressive externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool -- the Zacks Rank -- is a more conclusive indicator of a stock's near-term price performance, as it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. The size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, has resulted in a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) for AT&T.

title: Why Is Verizon (VZ) Up 7.4% Since Last Earnings Report?
detail:
Why Is Verizon (VZ) Up 7.4% Since Last Earnings Report?
Zacks Equity Research
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 10:30 AM EST 6 min read
VZ
^GSPC
T
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

A month has gone by since the last earnings report for Verizon Communications (VZ). Shares have added about 7.4% in that time frame, outperforming the S&P 500.

Will the recent positive trend continue leading up to its next earnings release, or is Verizon due for a pullback? Before we dive into how investors and analysts have reacted as of late, let's take a quick look at its most recent earnings report in order to get a better handle on the important catalysts.

VZ Beats Q3 Earnings Estimates on Strong Margins, Revenues Miss

Verizon reported adjusted earnings of $1.31 per share in the third quarter of 2026, up 8.3% year over year and ahead of the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $1.27 by 3.15%.

Total operating revenues increased 1.5% year over year to $34.31 billion but missed the consensus mark of $34.81 billion by 1.43%. Strong service revenue growth, improved operating efficiency and robust subscriber additions supported profitability. Verizon delivered 406,000 postpaid phone net additions, its strongest third-quarter performance in five years.

Service Revenues Grow Despite Equipment Weakness

Service revenues and other increased 3.5% year over year to $29.20 billion, supported by improving mobility and broadband trends. Wireless equipment revenues declined 9% to $5.12 billion, reflecting reduced upgrade activity and disciplined promotional spending.

Mobility and broadband service revenues reached $23.5 billion, increasing 2.9% year over year compared with 2.8% growth in the preceding quarter. Management attributed lower equipment sales to customers retaining devices longer and its strategy of reducing handset subsidies.

Consumer Segment Benefits From Service Growth

Consumer operating revenues increased 1.3% year over year to $26.43 billion. Mobility and broadband service revenues rose 3.6% to $19.78 billion, while wireless equipment revenues declined 10.3% to $4.28 billion. Other revenues grew 6% to $2.38 billion.

Consumer operating income improved 5.6% to $8.09 billion, with the operating margin expanding to 30.6% from 29.4%. Segment EBITDA increased 6.5% to $11.97 billion, while the corresponding margin improved 230 basis points to 45.3%.

Business Segment Records Higher Profitability

Business operating revenues rose 2.6% year over year to $7.02 billion. Mobility and broadband service revenues declined 0.8% to $3.71 billion, while wireless equipment revenues fell 1.6% to $839 million. Other revenues increased 10% to $2.47 billion.

Business operating income climbed 19.4% to $855 million, supported by lower selling, general and administrative expenses. Segment EBITDA advanced 13% to $1.94 billion, with the corresponding margin expanding to 27.6% from 25.1%.

Margins Expand Through Cost Discipline

Total operating expenses declined 0.2% year over year to $25.66 billion. Selling, general and administrative expenses decreased 3.5% to $7.48 billion, while wireless equipment costs fell 10.2%. However, depreciation and amortization expenses increased 10.3% to $5.10 billion.

Operating income rose 6.7% to $8.65 billion. Consolidated net income increased 5.2% to $5.32 billion, while net income attributable to Verizon improved 5% to $5.20 billion. Adjusted EBITDA increased 8% to a record $13.80 billion, with the adjusted EBITDA margin expanding 240 basis points to 40.2%. Interest expenses increased 17.2% to $1.95 billion.

Wireless Gains Offset Slower Broadband Additions

Verizon added 137,000 postpaid accounts, its best quarterly performance in more than a decade. Retail postpaid phone churn improved four basis points year over year to 0.94%, while Consumer postpaid phone churn declined to 0.87%.

Broadband net additions totaled 314,000, down from 322,000 a year earlier. Fiber broadband additions reached 155,000, while fixed wireless access contributed 159,000. Total broadband connections reached 17.4 million. The company also announced an agreement valued at more than $2 billion with Amazon Web Services to support AI infrastructure.

Cash Flow Strengthens Shareholder Returns

Third-quarter operating cash flow increased 2.2% year over year to $11.52 billion, while free cash flow improved 12.1% to $7.80 billion. Capital expenditures totaled $3.72 billion, compared with $4.31 billion a year earlier. For the first nine months, free cash flow increased 14.3% to $18.01 billion. Verizon returned $12.8 billion to shareholders through dividends and repurchases. Net unsecured debt stood at $123.72 billion, down from $128.68 billion in the preceding quarter. Net unsecured debt to adjusted EBITDA improved sequentially to 2.3 times.

VZ Raises 2026 Earnings and Subscriber Outlook

Verizon raised its 2026 adjusted earnings guidance to $5.04-$5.06 per share, implying 7%-7.5% year-over-year growth, compared with its previous projection of 6%-7%. The company increased its postpaid phone net additions forecast to 1.1 million-1.2 million. Mobility and broadband service revenue growth is expected in the upper half of the 2.5%-3% range, while free cash flow growth is projected to approach 12%. Capital expenditure guidance remains unchanged at $16-$16.5 billion.

You may still think of T-Mobile as the low-price carrier. Yet even as customers trade up, the stock lost about 18% in the twelve months to Tuesday, November 24, counting dividends. The S&P 500 returned 10.3% over the same dates.

So the question is whether richer accounts can lift a stock that has lagged the market. The stock closed at $167.30 on Tuesday. A price of $220 would be 31.5% above that close. That is just below the stock's highest close of the past year, $221.98 on February 24.

A rise that size has happened before. We took the largest rise from a close to a later close inside each calendar year, price only. That rise was 30% or more in 5 of the 10 calendar years from 2016 to 2025. The median of the ten yearly rises was 31%, just below the 31.5% that $220 needs. So a move to $220 sits inside the stock's own record, though the record is no promise.

What Is Lifting Revenue Per Account At T-Mobile US?

The driver is the revenue T-Mobile earns from each postpaid account. Postpaid customers pay a monthly bill, which is how most phone plans work. The average monthly revenue per account is called ARPA. In the quarter to September 2026, postpaid ARPA grew more than 4% from a year earlier, management said.

T-Mobile US shares still lost about 18% in a year while each account brought in more. If you hold the stock for steady income, that is a long fall to sit through while you wait for the price to come back. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.

Management also said existing customers keep a price edge. It said that "on average, our existing customers actually pay less than our new customers." So, on average, older customers still pay less than new ones. Management did not say how much of the ARPA gain came from changes to existing plans.

On the October 28 call, management raised its forecast for 2026 ARPA growth to about 3.5%. Its earlier forecast was 2.5% to 3%. It tied the change to premium plans, deeper customer relationships and what it called rate plan modernization.

The driver shows in the reported sales. Revenue was $93.8 billion in the four quarters to September 2026. That was 9.3% more than a year earlier. In the four quarters to September 2025, growth was 7.3%.

Does AT&T Look Undervalued on Earnings?

The P/E ratio works well for AT&T because earnings remain a key driver of how investors judge a mature telecom business. AT&T currently trades on a P/E of 11.8x, which is slightly below both the Telecom industry average of 14.4x and a touch under the peer group level of 11.9x. That positioning suggests the market is not assigning a premium for the group's profit stream, even with its scale and established customer base.

The Fair Ratio, which reflects what investors might typically pay for AT&T after factoring in its growth profile, margins, size and risks, sits meaningfully above the stock's current 11.8x multiple. This gap points to a valuation that screens as undervalued on this framework. Because the recent US$177m data breach settlement adds a clear risk overhang around cash outflows and trust, the discount implies the market may already be pricing in a portion of that concern.
